questions.question: What is the difference between JDK, JRE, and JVM?
questions.answer: The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) is the runtime engine that actually executes Java bytecode - it's an abstract machine specification implemented differently on each OS/architecture, and it's what gives Java its 'write once, run anywhere' behavior. The JRE (Java Runtime Environment) is the JVM plus the core class libraries (java.lang, java.util, etc.) and supporting files needed to run compiled Java programs - it's what an end user needs to run Java applications, but it has no compiler. The JDK (Java Development Kit) is a superset of the JRE that adds development tools like javac (the compiler), javadoc, jdb (debugger), and jar - it's what a developer needs to write and compile Java code. So the relationship is: JDK contains JRE, and JRE contains JVM. A common follow-up: you can run a .class file with just a JRE, but you need the JDK to compile a .java file.

questions.question: Why is Java considered platform-independent, and what role does bytecode play in this?
questions.answer: Java source code is compiled by javac into an intermediate, platform-neutral format called bytecode (.class files), not directly into machine code for a specific CPU/OS. That bytecode is then executed by the JVM, and it's the JVM implementation for each platform (Windows, Linux, macOS) that translates the same bytecode into native instructions for that platform. Because the bytecode itself never changes, the same compiled .class file or .jar can run unmodified on any machine that has a compatible JVM installed - this is the basis of Java's 'write once, run anywhere' (WORA) promise. Note that it's the bytecode that's portable, not the source code directly, and the JVM (not the language) is technically what is platform-specific.

questions.question: What are the different memory areas allocated by the JVM (heap, stack, method area, PC register, native method stack), and what is stored in each?
questions.answer: The JVM divides runtime memory into several distinct areas defined by the JVM specification: (1) Heap - shared across all threads, stores all objects and arrays created with 'new'; it's further divided into Young Generation (Eden + Survivor spaces) and Old/Tenured Generation for generational garbage collection. (2) Stack - one per thread, stores stack frames for method calls, each frame holding local variables, operand stack, and partial results; it grows and shrinks as methods are called and return, and throws StackOverflowError on excessive recursion. (3) Method Area (part of Metaspace since Java 8) - shared across threads, stores class-level data like the runtime constant pool, field/method metadata, and bytecode for methods. (4) PC (Program Counter) Register - one per thread, holds the address of the currently executing JVM instruction. (5) Native Method Stack - supports native (non-Java, e.g., C/C++ via JNI) method calls. Understanding this layout is key to explaining OutOfMemoryError (heap or metaspace exhaustion) versus StackOverflowError (stack exhaustion).

questions.question: Explain the Java classloader delegation model - how do the Bootstrap, Platform/Extension, and Application classloaders interact, and when would you need a custom classloader?
questions.answer: Java classloaders are arranged in a parent-first delegation hierarchy: the Application (System) ClassLoader is a child of the Platform ClassLoader (called the Extension ClassLoader before Java 9), which is a child of the Bootstrap ClassLoader (written in native code, loads core classes like java.lang.* from the runtime image, and has no parent). When a class needs to be loaded, the request starts at the Application loader but is delegated upward first: Application asks Platform, Platform asks Bootstrap. Bootstrap tries to find the class in the core JDK modules/rt.jar; if it can't, control falls back down to Platform, which checks its own sources (JDK platform modules); if it can't, control falls to Application, which searches the classpath; if that also fails, a ClassNotFoundException is thrown. This delegation model guarantees uniqueness (a class is loaded only once per loader) and prevents user code from shadowing core JDK classes (a form of sandboxing). You'd write a custom classloader when you need to load classes from non-standard sources - for example, loading classes over a network, from a database or encrypted file, implementing hot-reloading/plugin systems (as application servers like Tomcat do to isolate web apps from each other), or building an OSGi-style modular runtime. A custom loader typically extends ClassLoader and overrides findClass() (not loadClass(), so the default delegation logic is preserved).

questions.question: How does the JIT compiler improve performance over pure bytecode interpretation, and what is the difference between the C1 (client) and C2 (server) compilers?
questions.answer: The JVM starts out interpreting bytecode line-by-line, which is portable but slow. The JIT (Just-In-Time) compiler improves on this by profiling method execution at runtime and compiling 'hot' methods (ones called frequently) directly into native machine code, so subsequent calls skip interpretation entirely. HotSpot uses a tiered compilation strategy with two distinct compilers: C1 (the client compiler) compiles quickly with lighter optimizations and also inserts profiling instrumentation into the compiled code - it's optimized for fast warm-up and low compilation overhead. C2 (the server compiler) is much more aggressive: it uses the profiling data gathered by the interpreter/C1 to perform deep optimizations like method inlining, loop unrolling, and escape analysis, producing highly optimized code at the cost of longer, more CPU-intensive compilation. By default, modern HotSpot uses tiered compilation: methods move from interpreted -> C1 (tiers 1-3) -> C2 (tier 4) as they get hotter, giving both fast startup and eventual peak throughput. A key interview point: because of this warm-up behavior, JIT-compiled code can be deoptimized back to the interpreter if a speculative assumption (e.g., a branch that was 'never taken') turns out to be wrong - which is why microbenchmarks must discard the first few thousand iterations.

questions.question: What are Java's primitive data types, and what are their default values?
questions.answer: Java has 8 primitive types: byte (8-bit, default 0), short (16-bit, default 0), int (32-bit, default 0), long (64-bit, default 0L), float (32-bit floating point, default 0.0f), double (64-bit floating point, default 0.0d), char (16-bit Unicode character, default '\u0000'), and boolean (default false). These defaults apply only to instance and static (class-level) fields that aren't explicitly initialized - the JVM zero-initializes them. Local variables inside methods are NOT given a default value; the compiler requires them to be explicitly initialized before use, or it throws a compile-time error ('variable might not have been initialized'). This distinction between field defaults and local-variable-must-be-initialized rules is a common interview trap.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and .equals() when comparing objects?
questions.answer: == compares references for objects (i.e., whether two variables point to the exact same object in memory) and compares actual values for primitives. .equals() is a method defined on Object that, by default, also just does a reference comparison (same as ==) - but classes like String, Integer, and other wrapper/collection classes override it to compare logical/value equality instead. For example, new String("a") == new String("a") is false (two different objects) but new String("a").equals(new String("a")) is true (same characters). For custom classes, if you want 'meaningfully equal' objects (e.g., two Point objects with the same x/y) to be treated as equal, you must override equals() yourself (and hashCode() alongside it, to keep the contract required by hash-based collections).

questions.question: What is autoboxing and unboxing, and how can comparing boxed Integer values with == lead to subtle bugs?
questions.answer: Autoboxing is the compiler's automatic conversion of a primitive to its wrapper object (e.g., int -> Integer via Integer.valueOf()), and unboxing is the reverse (Integer -> int via intValue()). The bug: Integer.valueOf() maintains an internal cache of Integer objects for values from -128 to 127 (configurable up to a higher max via -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax). So Integer a = 100; Integer b = 100; means both autobox through valueOf(100), which returns the same cached object, making a == b true. But Integer a = 200; Integer b = 200; creates two distinct objects outside the cache range, so a == b is false, even though the values are equal. This is a classic interview gotcha because the code 'looks the same' at both value ranges but behaves inconsistently. The fix/best practice is to always use .equals() (or unbox to primitives before comparing) when comparing wrapper objects, and to prefer primitive int over Integer for simple arithmetic to avoid the overhead and confusion of boxing altogether. The same caching behavior exists for Byte, Short, Long (all -128 to 127) and Character (0 to 127), but only Integer's cache range is JVM-tunable.

questions.question: What are the four pillars of Object-Oriented Programming in Java?
questions.answer: The four pillars are: (1) Encapsulation - bundling data (fields) and the methods that operate on it into a single unit (a class), and restricting direct access to internal state via access modifiers (private fields with public getters/setters) so invariants can be protected. (2) Abstraction - exposing only essential behavior through interfaces or abstract classes while hiding implementation details, so callers depend on 'what' an object does rather than 'how'. (3) Inheritance - allowing a class (subclass) to acquire fields and methods from another class (superclass) via 'extends', enabling code reuse and establishing an 'is-a' relationship. (4) Polymorphism - the ability for the same method call to behave differently depending on the actual runtime type of the object, achieved via method overriding (runtime/dynamic polymorphism) and method overloading (compile-time/static polymorphism). A real-world example: a Shape interface (abstraction) with Circle and Square subclasses (inheritance) each overriding draw() (polymorphism), where each shape's internal fields are private (encapsulation).

questions.question: What is the difference between method overloading and method overriding?
questions.answer: Overloading happens within the same class when multiple methods share the same name but have different parameter lists (different number, type, or order of parameters) - it's resolved at compile time based on the reference type and arguments used, so it's a form of static/compile-time polymorphism. Overriding happens between a superclass and a subclass when the subclass provides a new implementation for a method with the identical signature (same name, parameters, and return type, or a covariant return type) - it's resolved at runtime based on the actual object type, making it dynamic/runtime polymorphism. Key distinctions: overloaded methods can have different return types and access modifiers freely; an overriding method cannot reduce visibility (e.g., can't override a public method as protected) and cannot throw broader checked exceptions than the method it overrides. Overloading is about 'many methods, same name, different signature, same class'; overriding is about 'same signature, different class hierarchy level, different behavior'.

questions.question: What is the difference between an abstract class and an interface in Java?
questions.answer: An abstract class can have both abstract methods (no body) and concrete methods with implementation, can declare instance fields with any access modifier and any state, and a class can extend only one abstract class (Java has no multiple class inheritance). An interface, historically, could only declare method signatures (implicitly public abstract) and constants (implicitly public static final) - but since Java 8 it can also have default methods (with a body, providing a default implementation subclasses can override) and static methods, and since Java 9 even private helper methods; a class can implement multiple interfaces. Use an abstract class when you want to share common state and code among closely related classes in an 'is-a' hierarchy; use an interface to define a contract/capability that unrelated classes can opt into (e.g., Comparable, Serializable), especially when you need multiple inheritance of type. A practical rule of thumb: 'favor interfaces for API contracts, abstract classes for shared implementation.'

questions.question: Why doesn't Java support multiple inheritance with classes, and how do interfaces help work around this limitation?
questions.answer: Java disallows a class from extending more than one class primarily to avoid the 'diamond problem': if class B and class C both extend class A and override the same method, and class D extends both B and C, the compiler cannot unambiguously decide which version of the method D should inherit. Rather than resolving this ambiguity with complex rules (as C++ does with virtual inheritance), Java's designers chose to keep single class inheritance for simplicity and predictability. Interfaces solve the need for 'multiple inheritance of type' safely: a class can implement multiple interfaces because, traditionally, interfaces carried no state and no implementation, so there was nothing to conflict over. Even with Java 8's default methods (which do carry implementation), the diamond problem is handled explicitly rather than silently: if a class implements two interfaces that provide conflicting default methods with the same signature, the compiler forces the class to override that method itself and explicitly choose (or combine) behavior using syntax like InterfaceName.super.methodName(), rather than picking one implicitly.

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between inheritance and composition when designing a class hierarchy, and why is "favor composition over inheritance" a common guideline?
questions.answer: Inheritance creates a tight, static 'is-a' coupling: a subclass automatically inherits (and depends on) the internal implementation details of its superclass, not just its public contract. This breaks encapsulation - if the superclass's internal implementation changes in a later version, subclasses can silently break even though they never touched that code (the 'fragile base class' problem). Inheritance is also fixed at compile time and single-rooted in Java, making it inflexible if a class later needs to 'behave like' two unrelated things. Composition instead builds a class by holding references to other objects and delegating to them ('has-a' relationship) through well-defined interfaces. This keeps coupling loose: the contained object can be swapped out, mocked in tests, or reconfigured at runtime, and changes to its internals don't ripple upward as long as its public contract is honored. The trade-off is that composition typically requires more boilerplate (explicitly writing delegating methods) compared to inheriting behavior for free. The 'favor composition over inheritance' guideline (popularized by Joshua Bloch's Effective Java) doesn't mean never use inheritance - it's appropriate for genuine, stable 'is-a' relationships (e.g., Circle is-a Shape) - but for code reuse across unrelated classes or when the relationship might change, composition combined with interfaces (strategy-pattern style) is more robust and testable.

questions.question: Can a static method be overridden in Java? Explain what actually happens when a subclass defines a method with the same signature as a static method in its parent.
questions.answer: No - static methods cannot be truly overridden because overriding relies on dynamic (runtime) dispatch based on the object's actual type, whereas static methods are resolved at compile time based on the reference type, since they belong to the class itself rather than to any instance. If a subclass declares a static method with the exact same signature as a static method in its parent, this is called 'method hiding', not overriding. The key practical consequence: if you call the method through a superclass-typed reference that actually points to a subclass object (Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod();), Java invokes the Parent's version, because the call is bound to the declared (reference) type, not the runtime type - this is the opposite of what happens with instance method overriding, where the Child's version would run. If you try to hide a static method with an instance method (or vice versa) in a subclass, the compiler throws an error, since Java requires this consistency.

questions.question: What is the difference between String, StringBuilder, and StringBuffer?
questions.answer: String is immutable - once created, its internal character sequence can never change; any operation that appears to modify a String (like concatenation) actually creates a brand-new String object, which is memory- and CPU-wasteful in loops. StringBuilder and StringBuffer are both mutable character sequences designed for efficient, repeated string manipulation. The difference between them is thread-safety: StringBuffer's methods are synchronized, making it safe for use across multiple threads but slower due to that synchronization overhead; StringBuilder (added in Java 5) has the identical API but is not synchronized, making it faster and the preferred choice in the vastly more common single-threaded use case. Rule of thumb: use String for fixed/rarely-changed text, StringBuilder for building/modifying strings in a single thread (e.g., inside a loop), and StringBuffer only if the same builder instance is genuinely shared and mutated across multiple threads.

questions.question: Why is the String class designed to be immutable in Java, and what benefits does this provide?
questions.answer: String immutability - meaning a String object's internal char/byte array can never be modified after construction - was a deliberate design choice for several reasons. First, security: Strings are used everywhere for sensitive data like class names, file paths, network hosts, and database URLs; if String were mutable, a malicious caller could change the value after it's been validated (e.g., after a security check on a file path) but before it's used, a class of vulnerability immutability eliminates. Second, it enables the String constant pool: since Strings never change, the JVM can safely have multiple references share the exact same underlying object for identical literal values, saving significant memory. Third, thread-safety: an immutable object can be freely shared across threads with no synchronization needed, since there's no way for one thread to see a partially-updated value. Fourth, safe use as a HashMap key: String's hashCode() is cached at first computation because the value can never change, making repeated hashing (e.g., for map lookups) cheap and guaranteeing the hash code never goes stale relative to the value - if Strings were mutable, mutating a String after using it as a map key would corrupt the map's internal bucket structure.

questions.question: What is the String constant pool, and how does the intern() method interact with it?
questions.answer: The String constant pool (also called the string intern pool) is a special memory region (part of the heap since Java 7, previously in PermGen) where the JVM stores unique String literal values so they can be shared/reused instead of duplicated. When you write String s = "hello";, the compiler checks the pool first: if "hello" already exists there, s is made to reference that existing object; if not, a new entry is added to the pool. This is why String a = "hello"; String b = "hello"; makes a == b true (both point to the same pooled object), but String c = new String("hello"); explicitly creates a new object on the regular heap outside the pool, so c == a is false even though c.equals(a) is true. The intern() method lets you manually opt an arbitrary String into the pool: calling c.intern() checks whether an equal value already exists in the pool - if so, it returns the pooled reference; if not, it adds c's value to the pool and returns that reference. This is useful for deduplicating large numbers of repeated dynamically-created strings (e.g., when parsing a big file with many repeated tokens) to save memory, though excessive interning can itself become a bottleneck since the pool has to be searched/maintained.

questions.question: What is a constructor, and how is it different from a regular method?
questions.answer: A constructor is a special block of code used to initialize a newly created object; it's invoked automatically when you use the 'new' keyword. Key differences from a regular method: a constructor must have the exact same name as its class and has no return type at all - not even void (unlike a method, which always has a return type). A constructor is called only once, implicitly, at the moment of object creation, whereas a regular method must be called explicitly and can be invoked any number of times. If you don't define any constructor, the compiler automatically inserts a no-argument 'default constructor' that calls the superclass's no-arg constructor - but this default is not generated if you've defined any constructor of your own. Constructors also cannot be inherited (though a subclass constructor can invoke a superclass constructor via super()), while methods can be inherited and overridden.

questions.question: What are the access modifiers in Java, and how do they differ in scope/visibility?
questions.answer: Java has four access levels, from most to least restrictive: (1) private - accessible only within the same class; not visible to subclasses or other classes, even in the same package. (2) default/package-private (no keyword) - accessible to any class within the same package, but not from outside the package. (3) protected - accessible within the same package, plus accessible from subclasses in other packages (via inheritance, though typically only through the subclass's own instance in some strict interpretations). (4) public - accessible from anywhere, no restrictions. These modifiers can be applied to classes, fields, methods, and constructors (top-level classes can only be public or default, not private/protected). A common design guideline is to make fields private and expose controlled access via public getters/setters (encapsulation), and to keep implementation classes/methods as restrictive as possible to minimize the public API surface.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a private constructor in Java, and where would you use one?
questions.answer: A private constructor prevents a class from being instantiated from outside the class itself (or, since inner/nested classes can access each other's private members, from certain closely related code). Common uses: (1) Singleton pattern - making the constructor private forces all access to go through a static factory method (e.g., getInstance()) that controls creation of the single shared instance. (2) Utility/helper classes that only contain static methods and constants (like java.lang.Math or java.util.Collections) - a private constructor (often throwing an AssertionError if somehow invoked via reflection) documents that the class is not meant to be instantiated at all, since instances would serve no purpose. (3) Static factory methods in general - a class might expose only named static creation methods (e.g., of(), from(), valueOf()) instead of a public constructor, giving more descriptive names, the ability to return cached/pre-built instances, or the ability to return a subtype, none of which a plain constructor allows.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array and an ArrayList in Java?
questions.answer: An array has a fixed size determined at creation time and cannot grow or shrink; an ArrayList is a resizable, dynamic data structure from the Collections framework that automatically grows its backing array as elements are added. Arrays can hold both primitives (int[], char[]) and objects, while an ArrayList can only hold objects (primitives must be autoboxed into their wrapper types, e.g., ArrayList<Integer>, which adds some memory/performance overhead). Arrays access elements with the concise [] syntax and offer slightly better raw performance for primitive-heavy workloads since there's no boxing and no method-call overhead, while ArrayList provides a much richer API (add, remove, contains, sort, stream support, etc.) at the cost of that overhead. In practice, use a plain array when the size is fixed and known upfront and you need maximum performance (e.g., numeric computation); use ArrayList for general-purpose collections where the size varies or you need the Collections framework's utility methods.

questions.question: What is the difference between ArrayList and LinkedList, and when would you choose one over the other?
questions.answer: ArrayList is backed by a dynamically resizable array, so random-access reads via get(index) are O(1), but inserting or removing an element in the middle requires shifting all subsequent elements, making that O(n). LinkedList is backed by a doubly-linked list of nodes, so get(index) is O(n) (it has to walk the list from the nearer end), but once you have a reference to a node (e.g., via an iterator, or operating at the head/tail), insertion and removal are O(1) since it's just pointer relinking - no shifting. LinkedList also implements the Deque interface, making it convenient for stack/queue-style usage (addFirst, removeLast, etc.). In practice, ArrayList is the better default for most use cases because modern CPUs favor array's cache locality (contiguous memory) even for many 'middle insertion' scenarios, and LinkedList's per-node object overhead (extra pointers, poor cache locality) often makes it slower in real benchmarks than its Big-O suggests. Choose LinkedList mainly when you have frequent insertions/removals at the ends or via an iterator and rarely need random access by index.

questions.question: What is the contract between equals() and hashCode(), and what breaks if you override one without the other?
questions.answer: The contract (defined in the Object class Javadoc) states: (1) if two objects are equal according to equals(), they MUST have the same hashCode(); (2) it is NOT required that unequal objects have different hash codes (collisions are allowed), though distinct hash codes improve hash table performance; (3) hashCode() must be consistent - calling it multiple times on the same unmodified object must return the same value within a single execution. If you override equals() but not hashCode(), you violate rule 1: two objects that your equals() says are equal can end up with different (default, identity-based) hash codes. The visible symptom is that hash-based collections break silently - for example, put an object into a HashSet or use it as a HashMap key, then try to look it up with an 'equal' but different object instance, and contains()/get() will return false/null, because the map computes a different bucket index from the (default) hash code and never even checks equals() against the object stored in the other bucket. The fix is simple but essential: always override equals() and hashCode() together, and derive both from the same set of significant fields (many IDEs and libraries like Lombok or Objects.hash() can generate this correctly).

questions.question: How does a HashMap store and retrieve key-value pairs internally, including how it handles hash collisions?
questions.answer: Internally, a HashMap holds an array of 'buckets' (Node<K,V>[] table). To store a key-value pair, it computes key.hashCode(), then applies an internal 'spread' function (XOR-ing the high and low bits of the hash) to reduce collisions from poor hashCode() implementations, and takes that result modulo the array length (implemented efficiently as a bitwise AND since the table size is always a power of two) to determine the bucket index. If that bucket is empty, the new Node is placed there directly. If the bucket already has entries (a collision), the new entry is appended to a linked list at that bucket (Java 8+: if that list grows past a threshold of 8 nodes AND the table itself has at least 64 buckets, the list is converted into a self-balancing red-black tree for that bucket, turning worst-case O(n) lookups into O(log n) - this defends against hash-flooding attacks and pathological hashCode() implementations). Retrieval (get) recomputes the hash, finds the bucket the same way, then walks the bucket's list/tree comparing hashCode() first (cheap) and then equals() (to confirm) until it finds a matching key. The default load factor is 0.75, meaning the table resizes (doubles) once it's 75% full, to keep the average bucket short and lookups close to O(1).

questions.question: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator in Java?
questions.answer: Comparable (java.lang.Comparable<T>) is implemented by the class whose instances you want to sort, and it defines a single method, compareTo(T other), representing that class's single 'natural ordering' (e.g., String's natural order is alphabetical, Integer's is numeric). Because there can only be one compareTo() implementation per class, a class has exactly one natural ordering. Comparator (java.util.Comparator<T>) is a separate object that defines an external, custom ordering via compare(T a, T b), and you can create as many different Comparators as you like for the same class (e.g., sort Employees by name, or by salary, or by hire date) without modifying the Employee class itself. Use Comparable when there's one obvious natural order for a type and you control that class's source code; use Comparator when you need multiple different orderings, need to sort a class you can't modify (e.g., a third-party library class), or want to compose/chain sort criteria (Java 8's Comparator.comparing().thenComparing() makes this very convenient).

questions.question: What is the difference between fail-fast and fail-safe iterators? Give an example of a collection that uses each.
questions.answer: A fail-fast iterator throws a ConcurrentModificationException immediately if the underlying collection is structurally modified (elements added or removed, not just value changes) while it's being iterated, other than through the iterator's own remove() method. It detects this using a 'modCount' counter that's incremented on every structural change and checked on each iterator.next() call. ArrayList, HashMap, and HashSet iterators are all fail-fast. A fail-safe iterator instead operates on a separate snapshot/clone of the collection's data (or, in the case of concurrent collections, tolerates concurrent structural changes without throwing), so it never throws ConcurrentModificationException, but it also means the iterator might not reflect the very latest state of the collection during iteration. CopyOnWriteArrayList and ConcurrentHashMap's iterators are fail-safe (weakly consistent) - CopyOnWriteArrayList literally iterates over an immutable snapshot array captured at iterator-creation time, while ConcurrentHashMap's iterator is designed to never throw and to reflect at least the state at creation time, possibly including some later updates. The trade-off: fail-fast gives you an early, loud signal of a concurrency/logic bug at the cost of throwing an exception; fail-safe favors availability/robustness for concurrent use cases at the cost of extra memory (for snapshotting) and potentially stale reads.

questions.question: Walk through what happens internally when a HashMap resizes (rehashing) once its load factor threshold is exceeded, and what the performance implications are.
questions.answer: A HashMap tracks a 'threshold' equal to capacity * loadFactor (default load factor 0.75, so a default 16-bucket map resizes once it holds more than 12 entries). When an insertion pushes the entry count past this threshold, the resize() method is triggered: the JVM allocates a brand-new bucket array with double the previous capacity (always a power of two, so bitmasking for bucket indices stays cheap), and then every existing entry must be rehashed and moved into the new, larger array - Java 8+ optimized this step cleverly: because capacity always doubles, each old bucket's entries split into exactly two new buckets (the original index, or original index + old capacity), determined by a single extra bit of the hash, so entries can be redistributed without recomputing the full hash for every key - just checking that one bit. Performance implications: resizing is an O(n) operation (must touch every existing entry), so it causes a noticeable latency spike on whichever put() call triggers it; if you know the approximate final size upfront, pre-sizing the HashMap via its constructor (new HashMap<>(expectedSize / 0.75)) avoids multiple resize-and-rehash cycles as the map grows organically. Also worth mentioning: if a bucket had treeified into a red-black tree (>=8 entries in that bucket, and >=64 total capacity), resizing may split and potentially un-treeify (revert to a linked list) if the split leaves fewer than 6 nodes in a resulting bucket.

questions.question: How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety with better performance than a synchronized HashMap or Hashtable?
questions.answer: Hashtable and Collections.synchronizedMap(new HashMap<>()) both use a single lock across the entire map, so only one thread can read or write at any given moment - this serializes all access and becomes a major bottleneck under concurrent load. Older ConcurrentHashMap implementations (pre-Java 8) improved on this with 'segment' locking, splitting the map into ~16 independently-locked segments so different threads could operate on different segments concurrently. Java 8 redesigned ConcurrentHashMap again and removed segments entirely, in favor of much finer-grained concurrency at the individual-bucket level: reads are completely lock-free (they traverse volatile-read node chains with no synchronization at all), and writes use Compare-And-Swap (CAS) to insert into an empty bucket without any locking; only when a bucket already has a colliding entry does the map fall back to a synchronized block, and crucially, that lock is scoped to just the head node of that one bucket, not the whole map or even a whole segment - so two threads writing to different buckets never contend at all. Table initialization and resizing are also done cooperatively via CAS, allowing multiple threads to help migrate entries to a new, larger table concurrently rather than blocking. Bonus detail: like a modern HashMap, buckets that collide heavily (>=8 entries) treeify into red-black trees for O(log n) worst-case lookups. The net effect is that ConcurrentHashMap scales to a very high number of concurrent readers and writers with far less contention than a single global lock.

questions.question: What is the difference between checked and unchecked exceptions in Java?
questions.answer: Checked exceptions are subclasses of Exception (excluding RuntimeException) and represent recoverable conditions the compiler forces you to explicitly handle - either by catching them in a try-catch block or declaring them in the method's throws clause - examples include IOException and SQLException. This is meant to force callers to consciously plan for predictable external failures (a file not existing, a network call failing). Unchecked exceptions are subclasses of RuntimeException (and Error) and are NOT checked by the compiler - you're not required to catch or declare them, though you certainly can - examples include NullPointerException, ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException, and IllegalArgumentException. These typically represent programming bugs or unrecoverable situations that could occur almost anywhere, so forcing every method to declare them would be impractical and would clutter code with meaningless throws clauses. A common interview follow-up: Error (like OutOfMemoryError or StackOverflowError) is also unchecked but represents serious JVM-level problems an application typically shouldn't try to catch/recover from.

questions.question: What is the difference between throw and throws in Java?
questions.answer: throw is a statement used inside a method body to actually raise/trigger a specific exception instance at that point in the code - for example, throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");. You can only throw one exception object at a time with a single throw statement. throws, on the other hand, is a clause used in a method's signature to declare that the method might propagate one or more checked exceptions up to its caller, without handling them itself - for example, public void readFile() throws IOException, FileNotFoundException. It doesn't actually raise an exception; it's purely a declaration/contract informing callers what they need to be prepared to catch or further propagate. In short: throw is an action performed in the method body, while throws is a declaration in the method signature - and throws is really only mandatory for checked exceptions, since the compiler doesn't require unchecked exceptions to be declared even if a method might throw them.

questions.question: What is try-with-resources, and how does it simplify resource management compared to a traditional try-finally block?
questions.answer: try-with-resources, introduced in Java 7, is a special form of the try statement that lets you declare one or more resources directly in the try's parentheses - any object that implements AutoCloseable (which Closeable, used by streams/readers/writers, extends). At the end of the block, Java automatically and implicitly calls close() on each declared resource, in reverse order of declaration, without needing an explicit finally block. Compared to manually writing try-finally, this eliminates a subtle but common bug: with nested resources in a traditional try-finally, if closing one resource throws an exception inside the finally block, it can silently mask/replace an earlier exception that was thrown in the try block, making the real root cause harder to diagnose. try-with-resources solves this with 'suppressed exceptions' - if the try block throws an exception and then closing a resource also throws, the original exception from the try block is the one propagated, and the close()-time exception is attached to it as a suppressed exception (retrievable via getSuppressed()), so no information is lost. Example: try (BufferedReader br = new BufferedReader(new FileReader(path))) { return br.readLine(); } - no finally, no manual close() calls, and correct handling even if multiple resources are declared.

questions.question: What are the differences between wait()/notify() and Thread.sleep(), and when would you use each?
questions.answer: wait() and notify()/notifyAll() are instance methods defined on Object (because every object has an intrinsic monitor lock) and are used for inter-thread communication/coordination: a thread calls obj.wait() inside a synchronized block on obj, which atomically releases the lock on obj and puts the thread into a WAITING state until another thread calls obj.notify() (wakes one waiting thread) or obj.notifyAll() (wakes all waiting threads) on that same object. Calling wait()/notify() outside a synchronized context throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Thread.sleep(millis), by contrast, is a static method on Thread that simply pauses the currently executing thread for a fixed duration - it does NOT release any locks the thread currently holds, and no other thread needs to 'wake it up'; it resumes automatically once the timeout elapses (or it's interrupted). Use wait()/notify() for classic producer-consumer style coordination, where one thread needs to wait for a specific condition that another thread will bring about (and you always guard the wait() call in a while loop re-checking the condition, to protect against spurious wakeups). Use sleep() simply to introduce a timed delay or polling interval without needing any cross-thread signaling, keeping in mind it holds onto any locks the whole time, which can create contention if used carelessly inside a synchronized block.

questions.question: What is the difference between a synchronized method and a synchronized block, and when would you prefer one over the other?
questions.answer: A synchronized method (public synchronized void foo()) locks on an implicit monitor for the entire duration of the method call: for an instance method, the lock is on 'this' (the current object); for a static synchronized method, the lock is on the Class object itself (a class-level lock). A synchronized block (synchronized(someObject) { ... }) lets you specify explicitly which object's monitor to lock, and lets you shrink the locked region to only the specific critical-section statements that truly need protecting, leaving the rest of the method unsynchronized. In practice, synchronized blocks are usually preferred because reducing the scope of the lock (only around the shared mutable state that's actually being read/modified) reduces contention and improves throughput - a synchronized method that does some expensive non-shared computation plus a tiny shared-state update forces every thread to serialize through the entire method unnecessarily. Synchronized blocks also let you lock on a dedicated private lock object instead of 'this', which is a defensive best practice, since locking on 'this' exposes your lock to external code that also happens to synchronize on the same object reference, risking unrelated contention or even deadlocks.

questions.question: What is the volatile keyword in Java, and what guarantees does it provide (and not provide)?
questions.answer: Declaring a field volatile gives two guarantees under the Java Memory Model: (1) Visibility - every write to a volatile field is flushed immediately to main memory, and every read of it is fetched fresh from main memory (bypassing CPU-core-local caches/registers), so a change made by one thread is guaranteed to be immediately visible to other threads that subsequently read the field. (2) Ordering - a write to a volatile field establishes a happens-before relationship with subsequent reads of that same field, which also prevents the compiler/JIT/CPU from reordering surrounding instructions across that volatile access in ways that would break this guarantee. What it does NOT provide: atomicity for compound operations. A classic example is count++ on a volatile int - this is actually three separate steps (read, increment, write), and two threads can interleave these steps and lose an update, even though each individual read/write is visible correctly. For atomic compound operations, you need synchronized blocks, explicit Locks, or Atomic classes like AtomicInteger (which use CAS internally). volatile is best suited for simple flags (e.g., a 'shutdown requested' boolean checked by a worker loop) or for safely publishing a reference set once (like the classic double-checked-locking singleton pattern), not for protecting multi-step invariants.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Runnable and Callable interfaces?
questions.answer: Runnable (part of java.lang since Java 1.0) defines a single method, void run(), which takes no arguments, returns nothing, and cannot throw any checked exception. Callable<V> (added in Java 5, part of java.util.concurrent) defines V call() throws Exception, which returns a typed result and is allowed to throw a checked exception. Because of this, Runnable is best for 'fire-and-forget' tasks where you don't need a result back (e.g., logging, a cleanup job), while Callable is the right choice when a task needs to compute and return a value, or when it might fail with a checked exception that the caller needs to observe. Both can be submitted to an ExecutorService, but only Callable, when submitted via submit(), gives you a Future<V> whose get() returns a meaningful computed result (a Future from a submitted Runnable just returns null on success); any exception thrown inside a Callable's call() is wrapped and surfaces to the caller as an ExecutionException when calling future.get(). Also, Thread's constructor accepts a Runnable directly (new Thread(runnable)), but there's no Thread constructor for Callable - it must go through an Executor (or be wrapped in a FutureTask, which itself implements Runnable).

questions.question: What are deadlock, livelock, and starvation? Describe a scenario that could lead to each.
questions.answer: All three are 'liveness' failures where a program fails to make progress, but they manifest differently. Deadlock: two or more threads are each permanently blocked, waiting on a resource held by the other - the classic example is Thread A holds Lock 1 and waits for Lock 2, while Thread B holds Lock 2 and waits for Lock 1; neither can ever proceed, and the threads sit blocked forever. The usual fix is enforcing a consistent global lock-acquisition order across all threads. Livelock: threads are NOT blocked - they're actively running and changing state, but their state changes keep responding to each other in a way that prevents real progress, like two people in a hallway who both repeatedly step the same direction to 'let the other pass' and keep bumping into each other; in software this often happens with overly-polite retry/backoff logic (e.g., two threads that both detect a conflict and both immediately release and retry, hitting the same conflict endlessly). Starvation: a thread is perpetually denied access to a resource it needs because other threads (often higher-priority or simply more aggressive) keep getting scheduled/access ahead of it - for example, if a lock implementation isn't fair and constantly grants access to whichever thread happens to request it next, a particular thread could theoretically wait indefinitely even though the lock is being actively used by others (not deadlocked, just unlucky forever). Fair locks (e.g., new ReentrantLock(true)) can mitigate starvation at some throughput cost.

questions.question: What is the difference between using an ExecutorService and manually creating and managing Thread objects?
questions.answer: Manually creating threads (new Thread(task).start()) means you're fully responsible for thread lifecycle management: creating, starting, and cleaning up threads yourself, with no built-in limit on how many you spawn (risking resource exhaustion under load), no easy way to get a result back from a thread, and no straightforward way to know when a task has finished other than join(). ExecutorService (from java.util.concurrent) abstracts this away by managing a pool of reusable worker threads: you submit tasks (as Runnable or Callable) to the pool via execute()/submit(), and the framework handles queuing tasks when all threads are busy, reusing threads across many tasks (avoiding the real cost of constantly creating/destroying OS threads), and returning a Future you can use to retrieve a result, check completion, or cancel the task. It also gives you centralized lifecycle control (shutdown(), shutdownNow(), awaitTermination()) and configurable pool sizing/queuing strategy (fixed, cached, scheduled, or a custom ThreadPoolExecutor) to match your workload and bound resource usage. In short, for anything beyond a single one-off background thread, ExecutorService is almost always preferred in production code because it's safer, more efficient (thread reuse), and gives you visibility and control that raw threads don't.

questions.question: Explain the Java Memory Model and the "happens-before" relationship - why does it matter for writing correct concurrent code?
questions.answer: The Java Memory Model (JMM), formalized in JSR-133, defines the rules for how and when writes made by one thread to shared memory become visible to reads made by another thread, in the presence of compiler optimizations, CPU instruction reordering, and per-core caching - all of which are allowed to reorder or delay memory operations for performance, as long as the program's observable single-threaded behavior isn't changed. Without any coordination, a variable written by Thread A might sit in that core's cache or register and never be visible to Thread B at all, or the compiler might reorder two independent writes such that Thread B observes them in a different order than they were written. The 'happens-before' relationship is the JMM's formal contract for when the model guarantees visibility and ordering across threads: if action X happens-before action Y, then the effects of X (including all writes made before it, by transitivity) are guaranteed visible to Y. Concrete happens-before rules include: (1) actions within a single thread happen-before each other in program order, (2) a monitor unlock happens-before every subsequent lock of that same monitor (this is why synchronized gives both mutual exclusion AND visibility), (3) a write to a volatile field happens-before every subsequent read of that field, (4) calling Thread.start() happens-before any action in the started thread, and (5) all actions in a thread happen-before another thread successfully returns from join() on it. This matters because without an established happens-before edge, two threads can legally observe shared state in ways that seem impossible from reading the source top-to-bottom - the classic broken example is a flag-based loop (while(!done) {}) with no synchronization or volatile, which a compiler may legally optimize into an infinite loop because it never proves 'done' can change from that thread's perspective. Understanding happens-before is what lets you reason correctly about which synchronization primitive (synchronized, volatile, java.util.concurrent classes) is sufficient for a given piece of shared-state code, rather than guessing.

questions.question: Why is double-checked locking for lazy Singleton initialization broken without the volatile keyword, and how does adding volatile fix it?
questions.answer: Double-checked locking is an optimization for lazy Singleton initialization that checks 'if instance == null' once without a lock (fast path for the common case where it's already initialized), and only acquires a lock and checks again if it appears null, to avoid the cost of synchronizing on every single getInstance() call. The classic bug: the line 'instance = new Singleton();' is not a single atomic operation from the JVM/compiler's point of view - it conceptually involves (1) allocating memory for the object, (2) invoking the constructor to initialize its fields, and (3) assigning the resulting reference to the 'instance' variable. Without volatile, the compiler or CPU is legally allowed to reorder steps (2) and (3), so another thread executing the unsynchronized first check could observe a non-null 'instance' reference that points to memory that hasn't finished running its constructor yet - that second thread would then use a partially-constructed object, potentially reading default/garbage field values, causing subtle and hard-to-reproduce bugs. Declaring the field as 'private static volatile Singleton instance;' fixes this because volatile, since JSR-133 (Java 5+), prevents this specific reordering (the write to the volatile reference cannot be reordered ahead of the writes that initialize the object it points to) and also ensures the fully-constructed reference is immediately visible to other threads once assigned. Without volatile (or an equivalent mechanism), double-checked locking is broken even though it 'usually works' in casual testing - it's a textbook example of why relying on the memory model matters, not just testing for observed correctness.

questions.question: How does the Fork/Join framework's work-stealing algorithm improve performance for divide-and-conquer parallel tasks?
questions.answer: The Fork/Join framework (java.util.concurrent, introduced in Java 7) is built around ForkJoinPool and tasks extending RecursiveTask<V> (returns a value) or RecursiveAction (returns nothing), each implementing a compute() method that recursively 'forks' (splits) a large problem into smaller subtasks once it's below some threshold, and 'joins' (waits for and combines) their results - a classic divide-and-conquer pattern, well suited to things like parallel merge sort, parallel array summation, or tree traversal. What makes ForkJoinPool distinctive versus a regular thread pool (ThreadPoolExecutor) is its work-stealing scheduler: rather than all worker threads pulling from one shared central queue (a potential contention point), each worker thread maintains its own double-ended queue (deque) of tasks. A thread pushes and pops its own new sub-tasks from the head of its own deque (LIFO order, which is cache-friendly since it processes the most recently created, most 'local' work first). When a worker thread runs out of tasks in its own deque, instead of sitting idle, it 'steals' work from the tail (opposite end) of another busy thread's deque - taking the oldest, typically largest, unclaimed chunk of work, which minimizes how often stealing needs to happen and reduces contention on that other thread's queue (since it operates on the opposite end from where the owning thread is working). This keeps all CPU cores continuously busy with minimal coordination overhead, dynamically load-balancing work even when subtasks have very uneven sizes/durations, which is why it significantly outperforms a naive fixed-partitioning approach for recursive, unevenly-sized workloads.

questions.question: What is the difference between CompletableFuture and a traditional Future, and how would you compose multiple asynchronous operations using it?
questions.answer: A plain Future (java.util.concurrent.Future, from Java 5) represents a pending asynchronous result but is very limited: the only way to retrieve the value is the blocking get() call (or a polling isDone() loop), there's no built-in way to attach a callback for when it completes, no way to combine/chain it with other Futures, and no way to complete it manually from outside or to signal failure with a custom exception path - once you're waiting on get(), you're just blocked. CompletableFuture (Java 8) implements both Future and the new CompletionStage interface, providing a rich, non-blocking, functional API for composing asynchronous pipelines. Key methods: thenApply(Function) transforms the result once available (like Stream's map) and returns a new CompletableFuture wrapping the transformed value; thenCompose(Function) is used when your callback itself returns another CompletableFuture, flattening the result instead of nesting Futures (like Stream's flatMap) - this is essential when chaining dependent async calls (e.g., fetch a user, then use that user's ID to fetch their orders); thenCombine(otherFuture, BiFunction) waits for two independent Futures and merges their results; allOf(...)/anyOf(...) wait for all or any of a group of Futures to complete; and thenAccept/exceptionally/handle let you attach success and error-handling callbacks that run asynchronously (on a common ForkJoinPool by default, or a supplied Executor) rather than blocking the calling thread. In short: Future tells you 'a result will exist eventually and you can wait for it'; CompletableFuture lets you declaratively build a whole pipeline of dependent, combined, and error-handled asynchronous steps without ever blocking a thread just to wait.

questions.question: What is a functional interface in Java, and how does it relate to lambda expressions?
questions.answer: A functional interface is any interface that declares exactly one abstract method (it may also have any number of default, static, or private methods, which don't count toward that limit) - examples include Runnable (run()), Comparator<T> (compare()), and the java.util.function package's Function<T,R>, Predicate<T>, Supplier<T>, and Consumer<T>. The @FunctionalInterface annotation is optional but recommended: it doesn't change behavior, but it makes the compiler enforce the single-abstract-method rule and documents intent, causing a compile error if someone later accidentally adds a second abstract method. Functional interfaces matter because they're the target type for lambda expressions and method references introduced in Java 8: a lambda like (a, b) -> a + b is really syntactic sugar that the compiler converts, at the call site, into an anonymous implementation of whatever functional interface is expected there (e.g., a BinaryOperator<Integer>) - the lambda's parameter list and body must match that single abstract method's signature. Without the concept of a functional interface providing that single well-defined method 'slot' to fill, the compiler wouldn't know what shape of code the lambda expression is supposed to represent, since Java is statically typed and lambdas have no explicit type of their own.

questions.question: What is the difference between intermediate and terminal operations in the Java Stream API?
questions.answer: Stream operations fall into two categories. Intermediate operations (like map(), filter(), sorted(), distinct(), limit()) transform one stream into another stream and are always lazy - they don't actually process any elements at the time they're called; they just build up a pipeline of transformations to be applied later. Because of this laziness, intermediate operations can be chained together fluently, and the stream can also apply optimizations like short-circuiting across the whole chain. Terminal operations (like collect(), forEach(), reduce(), count(), anyMatch(), toArray()) are what actually trigger the entire pipeline to execute: only once a terminal operation is invoked does the stream pull elements from the source and run them through every intermediate operation in the chain, one element at a time (rather than running map() over the whole collection, then filter() over the whole collection, etc.) - this element-by-element pipelining is why some short-circuiting terminal operations, like findFirst() or anyMatch(), can stop processing early without touching every source element at all. A key related fact: a Stream can only be consumed once - once a terminal operation has run, that stream object is 'closed' and calling another operation on it throws IllegalStateException; you must create a new stream from the source if you need to process it again.

questions.question: What is the purpose of Optional in Java 8, and how does it help avoid NullPointerException?
questions.answer: Optional<T> is a container object introduced in Java 8 that either holds a non-null value or represents the explicit absence of one (Optional.empty()), instead of a method returning a bare null to signal 'no result'. The core benefit is making the possibility of 'no value' visible and explicit in a method's return type/signature, forcing callers to consciously handle the empty case (e.g., via map(), filter(), orElse(), orElseGet(), or ifPresentOrElse()) rather than silently forgetting a null check and crashing later with a NullPointerException at some potentially distant, hard-to-trace call site. For example, a repository method 'Optional<User> findById(id)' documents at the type level that a user might not be found, whereas 'User findById(id)' returning null relies purely on convention/documentation that callers might miss. Common best practices: prefer Optional.ofNullable(value) over Optional.of(value) when the value might genuinely be null (of() throws NPE immediately if given null); avoid calling get() without first checking isPresent() (defeats the purpose, and throws NoSuchElementException on empty); and avoid using Optional as a field type or method parameter (its intended use is as a return type) since it doesn't serialize well and adds indirection where a simple null check or default value would do. It's worth noting Optional doesn't eliminate NullPointerException from the language - null can still exist everywhere else - it just gives you a much safer, more explicit tool for the common 'a value may be absent' pattern.

questions.question: What is type erasure in Java generics, and why did Java's designers choose this approach?
questions.answer: Type erasure is the mechanism by which the Java compiler enforces generic type constraints only at compile time, then strips out (erases) all generic type parameter information when generating bytecode, replacing type parameters with their bounds (Object, if unbounded) and inserting the necessary casts automatically. So List<String> and List<Integer> both compile down to the exact same raw List bytecode at runtime, with an implicit cast to String or Integer inserted wherever an element is retrieved. This is why you cannot do things like 'new T[10]' (can't instantiate a generic array type), 'if (obj instanceof List<String>)' (the JVM has no runtime knowledge of the <String> part - you can only check 'instanceof List'), or overload two methods that differ only by generic type parameter (e.g., void foo(List<String>) and void foo(List<Integer>) would erase to the identical signature and clash). Java's designers chose type erasure primarily for backward compatibility: generics were added in Java 5, and erasure allowed generic collections to be binary-compatible with the massive amount of pre-existing non-generic (raw-type) Java code and compiled libraries - a generic ArrayList<String> and an old raw ArrayList compile to interchangeable bytecode, so legacy code didn't need to be recompiled or rewritten to keep working alongside newer generic code.

questions.question: What is the difference between <? extends T> and <? super T> wildcards in generics, and when would you use each?
questions.answer: <? extends T> is an 'upper-bounded wildcard' meaning the type is T or any subtype of T; you use it when you only need to read items out of a generic structure, since it's guaranteed every element is at least a T (or more specific) - for example, a method that copies elements out of a List<? extends Number> can safely treat each element as a Number, but cannot safely add an arbitrary Integer or Double into that list, because the compiler doesn't know the list's actual concrete type parameter (it could be a List<Integer> at runtime, and adding a Double would corrupt it) - so extends effectively makes the structure read-only/'producer'. <? super T> is a 'lower-bounded wildcard' meaning the type is T or any supertype of T; you use it when you need to write T (or subtypes of T) into a generic structure, since any List<? super Integer> is guaranteed able to legally hold an Integer (whether it's actually a List<Integer>, List<Number>, or List<Object>) - but reading from it only safely gives you back an Object, since the compiler can't know the specific supertype. This is formalized in the mnemonic PECS - 'Producer Extends, Consumer Super': use extends for a generic parameter you're only reading from (producing values for your code), and super for one you're only writing into (consuming values from your code) - the classic example is Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src).

questions.question: At a high level, how does generational garbage collection work in the JVM (young generation, old generation, minor vs major GC)?
questions.answer: Generational garbage collection is based on the empirical observation ('the weak generational hypothesis') that most objects die young - the vast majority of allocated objects become garbage very quickly (e.g., temporary variables, short-lived request objects), while a much smaller set survives long-term. To exploit this, the JVM heap is split into a Young Generation (further divided into an Eden space, where new objects are first allocated, and two Survivor spaces, S0/S1, used alternately) and an Old (Tenured) Generation for long-lived objects. New objects are allocated in Eden; when Eden fills up, a Minor GC runs, which is fast because it only scans the small young generation - live objects are copied out of Eden (and the currently-active Survivor space) into the other, currently-empty Survivor space, and each surviving object's 'age' counter is incremented. Once an object survives enough minor GC cycles (reaching a tenuring threshold), it's 'promoted' into the Old Generation, on the assumption it's likely to live a long time. A Major (or Full) GC scans and reclaims the Old Generation (often the whole heap, including young gen, and can also include metaspace), which is far more expensive since the old generation is typically much larger - this is the pause type most likely to cause noticeable application latency spikes ('stop-the-world' pauses), which is why modern collectors (G1, ZGC, Shenandoah) focus heavily on minimizing old-generation/full-GC pause times through concurrent and incremental collection strategies rather than always doing a single long stop-the-world sweep.

questions.question: How would you diagnose and fix a Java application experiencing frequent full GC pauses or an eventual OutOfMemoryError in production?
questions.answer: Start with data, not guesses. Enable GC logging (e.g., -Xlog:gc*:file=gc.log with modern unified logging, or -verbose:gc/-XX:+PrintGCDetails on older JVMs) and use jstat -gcutil <pid> for a live view of heap-region occupancy and collection counts/timings - a pattern of frequent, back-to-back full GCs that reclaim very little heap each time is the classic signature of either a genuine memory leak or a heap sized too small for the working set. Next, capture a heap dump - ideally automatically at the moment of failure via -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/path, or manually with jmap -dump - and analyze it in a tool like Eclipse Memory Analyzer (MAT) or VisualVM; MAT's 'Leak Suspects' report and dominator tree are specifically designed to show which object (or object graph, often a collection that's growing unbounded, like a cache with no eviction policy, an ever-growing static Map, or unclosed resources/listeners that keep objects reachable) is retaining the most memory and preventing collection. If threads also appear stuck/blocked around the same time, a thread dump (jstack <pid> or kill -3) helps correlate - for example, GC pressure sometimes causes contention/backups elsewhere in the system that look unrelated at first. Once the root cause is identified, the fix is usually one of: correcting a genuine leak (bounding a cache with an eviction policy or switching to a WeakHashMap/soft references where appropriate, closing resources properly, removing listener references), tuning heap sizing/generation ratios (-Xmx, -Xmn) to better match the actual working set and allocation rate, or switching garbage collectors (e.g., moving to G1 or ZGC) if pause times themselves - rather than a leak - are the core problem for a large heap under strict latency SLAs. The key interview point is the methodology: logs/metrics to confirm the symptom, heap dump analysis to find the actual retained object graph, then a targeted fix - not blindly increasing heap size, which often just delays the same OutOfMemoryError.

questions.question: What are the different reference types in Java (strong, soft, weak, and phantom), and how are they used to build memory-sensitive caches or avoid memory leaks?
questions.answer: Java's java.lang.ref package defines four reference strengths, from strongest to weakest: (1) Strong reference - the default kind (Object o = new Object();); as long as any strong reference chain reaches an object, the garbage collector will never reclaim it, no matter how much memory pressure exists. (2) SoftReference - wraps a referent that the GC is guaranteed to reclaim only if the JVM is genuinely running low on memory; the spec guarantees all soft references are cleared before an OutOfMemoryError would otherwise be thrown. This makes SoftReference ideal for memory-sensitive caches: you get the benefit of caching (avoiding recomputation/re-fetching) as long as memory allows, but the cache automatically shrinks under pressure instead of causing an OOM itself. (3) WeakReference - the referent is eligible for collection as soon as no strong references to it remain, regardless of memory pressure (the GC doesn't wait for pressure - it clears these eagerly on the next collection cycle). This is used for canonicalizing mappings and metadata that should disappear the moment the 'real' object does - the built-in WeakHashMap wraps its keys in WeakReferences precisely so entries are auto-removed once their key is otherwise unreferenced, which is useful for caches/registries keyed by objects whose lifecycle you don't fully control (e.g., avoiding classloader leaks by holding class metadata keyed weakly). (4) PhantomReference - the weakest kind; get() always returns null (you can never retrieve the referent through it), and it's enqueued onto a ReferenceQueue only after the object has already been finalized and is about to have its memory reclaimed - it's used purely to schedule pre-mortem cleanup actions (like releasing native/off-heap resources) at a well-defined point, more reliably than the deprecated finalize() mechanism. In short: strong = normal Java references; soft = 'keep unless memory is tight' (caches); weak = 'discard as soon as nothing else needs it' (canonical/metadata maps, avoiding leaks); phantom = 'notify me right before this memory is actually freed' (deterministic cleanup).

questions.question: How would you design a thread-safe, high-performance LRU cache in Java from scratch, and what concurrency considerations would you need to handle?
questions.answer: A single-threaded LRU cache is straightforward: a HashMap for O(1) key lookup combined with a doubly-linked list (or Java's built-in LinkedHashMap constructed with accessOrder=true, overriding removeEldestEntry() to auto-evict) to track recency order, giving O(1) get and put by moving the accessed/inserted node to the 'most recently used' end and evicting from the 'least recently used' end when over capacity. The complexity is in making this thread-safe without destroying performance. The simplest approach - wrapping a LinkedHashMap with a single ReentrantLock or synchronized methods (or Collections.synchronizedMap) - is correct but serializes all access through one lock, becoming a bottleneck under high concurrency since even reads (get) must mutate the recency ordering (moving the node), so you can't cheaply make reads lock-free the way ConcurrentHashMap does for a plain map. A more scalable design uses a ConcurrentHashMap<K, Node<K,V>> for the actual key-to-node storage (giving fast, low-contention lookups) combined with a separate mechanism for recency tracking - either a concurrent doubly-linked list with fine-grained per-node locks (or lock-free CAS-based linking) that only locks the small neighborhood of nodes being relinked during a move-to-front, or a ConcurrentLinkedDeque tracking access order, carefully coordinated with the map so that eviction and recency updates on the two structures stay consistent (this coordination is the trickiest correctness issue - you must avoid a race where a node is being evicted by one thread while another thread is simultaneously 'touching'/promoting that same node). Key concurrency considerations to discuss: (1) atomicity of the combined 'update the map AND update the recency structure' operation, (2) whether reads should require a lock at all (a common relaxation is 'approximate' LRU that only updates recency periodically/probabilistically to avoid locking on every single read, trading strict LRU-accuracy for throughput), and (3) eviction policy under concurrent capacity pressure. In practice, for production systems, most engineers would point out that battle-tested libraries like Caffeine (which uses a lock-free ring-buffer-based approach for recording access events, batching recency updates off the hot path) or Guava's Cache solve exactly this problem far more robustly than a hand-rolled implementation, and would only hand-roll one in an interview to demonstrate understanding of the underlying trade-offs.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the transient keyword in Java serialization?
questions.answer: The transient keyword marks a field so that it is skipped entirely during Java's default serialization process - when an object is serialized (written to a byte stream via ObjectOutputStream), any field marked transient is simply omitted from that stream, and on deserialization it comes back with its default value (null for objects, 0/0.0/false for primitives) rather than its original value. This is used for two main reasons: (1) excluding sensitive data that shouldn't be persisted or transmitted, such as a password or an API key held temporarily in memory, and (2) excluding fields that are either not meaningful across JVM instances (like a Thread, Socket, or file handle) or that can be cheaply recomputed after deserialization (like a cached derived value) rather than wastefully serialized. Note that transient only affects the default Serializable mechanism - if a class implements Externalizable instead and writes its own writeExternal()/readExternal() logic, the transient keyword has no effect at all, since the programmer controls the entire process manually.

questions.question: What is serialVersionUID, and what happens during deserialization if the sender's and receiver's serialVersionUID don't match?
questions.answer: serialVersionUID is a static final long field that acts as a version identifier for a Serializable class, used to verify that the sender (the class that serialized an object) and the receiver (the class trying to deserialize it) agree on the class's shape. If you don't declare one explicitly, the JVM computes one implicitly at compile/runtime by hashing structural details of the class (name, implemented interfaces, field names/types/modifiers, method signatures) using an algorithm defined in the Object Serialization Specification (retrievable via the serialver tool) - which means this computed value can silently change if you make almost any change to the class (adding a field, changing a method), even ones that wouldn't otherwise break compatibility. During deserialization, the JVM compares the serialVersionUID embedded in the serialized byte stream against the serialVersionUID of the currently loaded class; if they don't match, it throws InvalidClassException and deserialization fails immediately. Best practice is to always declare serialVersionUID explicitly as a constant: this way, additive/compatible changes (like adding a new field, which just gets a default value on old data) don't break deserialization of previously-serialized objects, whereas truly incompatible changes (removing a field, changing a field's type, changing the class hierarchy) still require a new UID or accept that old serialized data can no longer be read.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Serializable and Externalizable interfaces in Java?
questions.answer: Serializable is a marker interface - it has no methods at all, and simply implementing it tells the JVM 'use the default, automatic serialization mechanism' (implemented internally via reflection to walk and write every non-transient, non-static field). Externalizable extends Serializable but adds two methods you must implement yourself: writeExternal(ObjectOutput) and readExternal(ObjectInput), giving the class - not the JVM - full manual control over exactly what bytes get written and how they're reconstructed. Key practical differences: with plain Serializable, the transient keyword controls what's excluded, and no constructor is called during deserialization (fields are set directly via reflection); with Externalizable, transient has no effect since you write the logic yourself, and critically, the class's public no-argument constructor IS called during deserialization before readExternal() populates the fields (so an Externalizable class must have an accessible no-arg constructor, or deserialization fails). Externalizable is chosen when you need better performance (default reflection-based serialization is relatively slow) or precise control over format/versioning/security (e.g., deliberately excluding or encrypting certain fields), at the cost of significantly more code and responsibility for maintaining backward compatibility yourself.

questions.question: What is Java Reflection, and what are some common use cases (and risks) of using it?
questions.answer: Reflection (java.lang.reflect) is the API that lets a running Java program inspect and manipulate its own classes, fields, methods, and constructors at runtime, even without compile-time knowledge of the exact type involved - for example, obj.getClass().getDeclaredFields() lists every field a class declares, and Method.invoke() can call a method dynamically by name. Common use cases: frameworks like Spring and Hibernate use it heavily to instantiate beans, inject dependencies, and map object fields to database columns based on annotations, without the framework author needing to know your classes at compile time; testing frameworks like JUnit use it to discover and invoke @Test-annotated methods; and it's the mechanism behind many serialization and dependency-injection libraries. The risks: (1) performance - reflective calls bypass many JIT optimizations and involve extra runtime checks, making them notably slower than direct calls, especially in hot code paths; (2) it breaks encapsulation - setAccessible(true) lets you read/write even private fields and invoke private methods, defeating the access-control guarantees a class's author relied on; (3) it trades compile-time safety for runtime errors - a typo in a field/method name that reflection looks up by String will only surface as a NoSuchFieldException or NoSuchMethodException at runtime, not a compile error; and (4) it makes code harder to statically analyze, refactor safely (an IDE 'rename method' won't catch a reflective String lookup), and reason about.
